newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ sets conference to ponder migration, population.
newsitem.headline: NZ sets conference to ponder migration, population.

text.p: New Zealand on Wednesday set the dates for a conference intended to ponder future directions for population change and immigration.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger said in a statement the conference, which was proposed as part of the agreement that brought his centre-right coalition government to power, should address the country's "profound" recent demographic changes.
"There has been a marked decrease in fertility rates, an increase in one-parent families, and a growth in the number of settlers from non-European countries (in the past two decades)," he said.
The conference will take place in the new Museum of New Zealand in Wellington on November 13 and 14.
Treasurer Winston Peters, who leads the coalition's junior partner, the nationalist New Zealand First party, said the conference would also look at the economic impact of change.
Peters, of Maori-European heritage, campaigned heavily in last year's election against immigration, particularly from Asia.

"(It) is an opportunity for New Zealand to explore the relationship between population change and immigration on economic activity and future demand for education, social services and business " he said.

New Zealand is a country formed by immigration, from Maori settlers many centuries ago through Anglo-European settlers in the 19th and early 20th centuries, to post-war waves of Southeast Asian and Pacific Island migrants.
While Maori now make up 14.5 percent of the population, or about 523,000 people, officials estimate that about another 10 percent speak languages other than English or Maori as a first language.

Part of the aim of the conference is to underpin future policies, which the coalition has said should reflect the country's needs in terms of skills and "the ability of the community to absorb" new migrants.

Asia 2000, a lobby group that promotes understanding between New Zealand and the Asian region, has welcomed the conference, but warned that Wellington should ensure its policies continue to be seen as fair and equitable.

"Asian immigration cannot be looked at just as a domestic issue here, but rather as one tightly interwoven into the multifaceted relationship New Zealand has developed with the countries of the region," its executive director Phillip Gibson said recently.
He said there was a need for extreme care "to ensure that a legitimate debate about immigration is not perceived in the region as a camouflage for a debate about race".
